subsystems.name: Sensing chemistry
subsystems.role: turns the concentration of a molecule into an electrical signal.

subsystems.name: Skin interface
subsystems.role: keeps the sensor in contact with interstitial fluid without causing irritation or infection.

subsystems.name: Readout electronics
subsystems.role: measures tiny currents, averages noise and stores readings.

subsystems.name: Analytics
subsystems.role: turns a stream of numbers into a personal baseline and flags departures from it.
parts: other wearable inputs such as heart rate and temperature

subsystems.name: Data and alerting layer
subsystems.role: stores the history, compares it with reference data and routes warnings to the user or a clinician.

buildSteps.title: Pick the analytes
buildSteps.detail: Choose which molecules to track — glucose is the only one with mature continuous sensing; lactate, ketones, electrolytes and inflammatory markers are candidates but far less proven.

buildSteps.title: Design the sensing chemistry
buildSteps.detail: For each target, select an enzyme, aptamer or ion-selective membrane that reacts specifically with it and produces a measurable current or voltage.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the sensor
buildSteps.detail: Microneedles or thin-film electrodes are patterned by etching or lithography, then coated with the recognition layer and a protective membrane that resists fouling by proteins.

buildSteps.title: Bench-test in vitro
buildSteps.detail: Sensors are soaked in synthetic interstitial fluid to measure sensitivity, response time, drift and cross-sensitivity to similar molecules.

buildSteps.title: Package and sterilise
buildSteps.detail: The sensor is mounted in a patch with its electronics, sealed against moisture and sterilised for skin contact.

buildSteps.title: Validate against blood
buildSteps.detail: Clinical studies compare sensor readings with laboratory blood draws over days, across people and skin types.

buildSteps.title: Learn a personal baseline
buildSteps.detail: The device runs for a stretch of healthy days so the model can learn what is normal for this individual, since absolute concentrations vary widely between people.

buildSteps.title: Fuse signals and set thresholds
buildSteps.detail: The algorithm combines chemistry with heart rate, temperature and sleep, then is tuned so that it warns early without drowning the user in false alarms.

buildSteps.title: Clear it and wire it into care
buildSteps.detail: Regulatory review and clinician workflows decide what happens when the device says something is wrong — a step where most such systems stall.

prerequisites.why: the only continuous molecular monitor in wide use; it proves the subcutaneous sensing principle but only for one molecule.
measuring several analytes stably for days or weeks in living tissue remains a research problem.
a patch must run for days on a small battery while sampling and transmitting.

prerequisites.tech: Longitudinal datasets linking physiology to disease onset
prerequisites.why: reference data exist for heart rhythm and glucose, but far less for the broader chemistry-and-illness link.
showing that a signal change precedes symptoms, and that acting on it improves outcomes, is largely unproven.

pathway.milestone: continuous glucose monitors plus wrist-worn heart-rate and temperature sensors
pathway.unlocks: real-time tracking of one molecule and general physiological trends.

pathway.milestone: multi-analyte patches that hold calibration for a week or more
pathway.unlocks: monitoring beyond diabetes, such as in hospital or post-surgical care.

pathway.milestone: prospective trials showing that alerts change clinical outcomes
pathway.unlocks: regulatory clearance for illness prediction rather than just measurement.

pathway.milestone: integration into routine care and, cautiously, consumer use
pathway.unlocks: shifting some medicine from episodic testing to continuous surveillance — raising open questions about false alarms, privacy and anxiety.
